title: Genuina principia doctrinae de statu aequilibrii et motu corporum tam perfecte flesibilium quam elasticorum

deep.reconstruction:
The page has three parts.

(1) It finishes §XIX: a uniform elastic rod whose natural (unstressed) shape is a circular arc of radius a. On the previous page Euler set the bending moment to Vv = A(φ' − 1/a). He then derived the shear force V = Aφ'' and the tension T in two ways: T = ∫p ds − Aφ'^2/2 from the tangential balance, and T = (Aφ''' − q)/φ' from the normal balance. Equating the two gives a differential equation for the curve. Euler observes that this final equation does not contain a. The natural radius enters only through the constants of integration, because the moment Vv must be prescribed at the ends of the rod. In modern terms: a constant intrinsic curvature changes the bending moment only by the constant A/a. The moment enters the force balances only through its derivative, the shear force V, so the field equations are those of an initially straight rod. The natural curvature affects only the boundary conditions on the moment.

(2) §XX ('Applicatio ad casus particulares') restates the loading assumption. Every load acting on the element Mm = ds of a plane curve is resolved into a tangential component p ds along mMT and a normal component q ds along mn. Out-of-plane forces are excluded because only plane curves are considered.

(3) §XXI introduces Cartesian coordinates: abscissa AX = x and ordinate XM = y, with ds = √(dx² + dy²). With φ the angle XMT between the ordinate and the tangent, the element angle is Tmt = dφ, the same quantity used earlier. Hence sin φ = dx/ds and cos φ = dy/ds, i.e. dx = ds sin φ and dy = ds cos φ.

This prepares §XXII (next page). There fixed-direction loads P and Q are converted into p = P sin φ + Q cos φ and q = Q sin φ − P cos φ, and the catenary is then treated as Problem I.
errors: Nothing on this page is wrong. The statement that the final equation is independent of a is correct.

Neighbouring page (§XVIII, as transcribed): from Vv = A(dφ/ds − 1/r) and V = A(ddφ/ds² + dr/(r² ds)) one gets v = r ds(r dφ − ds)/(r² ddφ + ds dr), with a plus sign in the denominator. The transcription shows a minus. This is either a transcription slip or a sign error in the print; it does not affect §XIX, where dr = 0.

ideas.what: A constant natural curvature drops out of the equilibrium equations of a uniform elastica and enters only through the end moments.
ideas.modern_name: Intrinsic (spontaneous) curvature in Euler–Bernoulli / Kirchhoff rod theory; constant intrinsic curvature affects only the moment boundary conditions.
ideas.usually_credited_to: Euler (in this paper, E410, and earlier remarks on naturally curved lamina); standard in later rod theory (Kirchhoff, Clebsch, Love)
ideas.where_published: E410, Novi Commentarii 15 (1771), §§XVII–XIX; discussed by Truesdell, Rational Mechanics of Flexible or Elastic Bodies (Opera omnia II 11/2)

ideas.what: Resolution of distributed loads into tangential and normal components per unit arc length.
ideas.modern_name: Intrinsic (Frenet-type) force balance for strings and rods
ideas.where_published: E410 and many earlier Euler papers on flexible lines

ideas.what: Relation of the tangent angle to Cartesian coordinates: dx = ds sin φ, dy = ds cos φ.
ideas.modern_name: Tangent-angle parametrization of a plane curve

deep.surprise_reason: The page is transitional bookkeeping. Its one substantive remark, that a naturally circular rod obeys the same field equations as a straight one, is correct and already part of Euler's known treatment of rods with natural curvature, which Truesdell surveyed.
transcription_corrections: 'et et mn = dy': the duplicated 'et' at the line break is in the original print, not a transcription error.
The opening of §XIX's conclusion on this page reads 'vnde patet aequationem finalem non inuoluere quantitatem a'; the transcription is correct.
